characters: Roland Bampoe: a 14-year-old boy in a school uniform, holding a hand lens above a cocoa flower.
Mrs Amoo: the agriculture teacher, in a work apron and straw hat, with a small pot of leaf litter.
Marvin Coleman: Roland’s friend and school-magazine editor, with a notebook and a pen.
The cocoa tree: a cocoa tree under taller shade trees, with tiny pink-white flowers growing straight from the trunk and large pods beside them.

narrationPlan.voice: Eager boy’s voice for Roland; a patient, curious voice for Mrs Amoo; a friendly voice for Marvin
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and quietly amazed, slowing for the tiny details (about 118 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Gentle, buzzing marimba with soft farm sounds; a warm, wondering tune at the discovery (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Roland, Mrs Amoo, Marvin and the school are invented. The cocoa facts come from the Natural History Museum’s article on cocoa pollinators: biting midges (family Ceratopogonidae, genus Forcipomyia) are the main pollinators; they are about one to three millimetres long; cocoa flowers grow on the trunk, cannot self-pollinate and last one or two days; roughly one in 400 to 500 flowers sets fruit and 10 to 30 per cent of young pods mature; larvae live in damp rotting wood and leaf litter; clearing shade trees harms midge habitat.
The story does not say that all clearing is wrong. It also shows that reports differ on how much of Ghana’s forest loss is due to cocoa expansion and how much to logging, mining and other farming.
The story gives only simple steps (keep some shade trees, leave leaf litter) and tells readers to ask their agricultural extension officer; it does not give yield figures.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have an agricultural officer or a cocoa researcher check the pollination facts and the advice on shade and leaf litter against current practice and COCOBOD or CRIG guidance.
Check the statement that cocoa flowers make no nectar and that midges pollinate by accident (page 3) against a cocoa pollination source.
Check the article-writing tip against the NaCCA English syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about the tiny pollinators of cocoa and what they need. It links forests, farms and food and models a school-magazine article.
learningGoals: Explain what pollinates cocoa and what it needs to live.
Describe two steps a farmer can take to help.
Write a short article with a headline, byline and a clear closing line.
beforeReading: Ask: where does chocolate come from? What does a cocoa flower need to become a pod?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to name the three things midges need.
afterReading: Observe leaf litter with a hand lens (outdoors, with an adult) and sketch what you see.
Write a magazine article about a small animal that helps your family farm.
discussion: Why might a farmer clear shade trees? What are other options?
How does a tiny insect connect a forest to a chocolate bar?
reflection: Which small creature on your farm or compound do you rarely notice?

mathsExtension.task: If one flower in 450 sets fruit, how many pods might 9,000 flowers produce?
If 20 per cent of 50 young pods mature, how many mature?

support: Provide an article frame: HEADLINE, byline, opening line, two facts, one cause and effect, closing line.
stretch: Write a letter to the District Agricultural Officer asking for advice on shade trees for a cocoa farm.
